We treated a 57-year-old woman with a type
B1 thymoma, based on the World Health Organization
classiﬁcation, who had stiff man syndrome. Her symp-
toms were alleviated after a thymectomy. Herein we
report a case of stiff man syndrome with a thymoma and
also review three cases reported previously.
(Ann Thorac Surg 2005;80:739 – 41)

S
tiff man syndrome is a rare neurologic disorder, ﬁrst
described in 1956 by Moersch and Woltman [1]. The
chief symptoms of the disease are muscle rigidity and
cramps, which are thought to result from immune-
mediated inhibition of catecholamine excitatory and r-
aminobutyric acidergic neuron function. Further, 60% of
patients with stiff man syndrome are reported to have
antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). In
some cases, this syndrome occurs in association with
other autoimmune diseases, such as insulin-dependent
diabetes mellitus, Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis,
and pernicious anemia, whereas in others, the disease
shows a paraneoplastic nature with manifestations of
breast cancer, mediastinal tumors, thymoma, small cell
lung cancer, Hodgkin disease, and colon cancer [2].
Herein we report a case of stiff man syndrome with a
thymoma and also review three cases reported previ-
ously [3–5].
A 57-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital in
February 2001 with symptoms of continuous muscle
stiffness and painful muscle spasms, which began as
tightness in the upper limbs and deteriorated into muscle
stiffness of the trunk and lower limbs 1 month after onset.
At her ﬁrst visit to our department, she was unable to
maintain a standing or sitting position. She had no
history of diabetes, injuries, or epilepsy. A laboratory
examination and serum biochemical study including se-
rum tumor markers also revealed nothing abnormal.
However, another laboratory examination disclosed an
extremely high titer of the anti-GAD antibody in serum
at 16,800 U/mL (normal range, /H110211.5), suggesting a diag-
nosis of stiff man syndrome. The patient was treated with
baclofen and diazepam, and her symptoms of continuous
muscle stiffness and painful muscle spasms were re-
lieved but were easily evoked by tactile stimulation. A

computed tomography of the chest was conducted,
which revealed an anterior mediastinal tumor that was
considered to be a thymoma ( Fig 1), and suggested that
her symptoms were caused by a paraneoplastic neuro-
logic syndrome associated with a thymoma. We per-
formed an extended thymectomy with wedge resection of
the left upper lobe of the lung and a partial pericardec-
tomy in May 2001. A histologic examination revealed the
thymoma to be predominantly a lymphocytic type, which
was type B1 tumor according to the World Health Orga-
nization (WHO) classiﬁcation [6], with no invasion of the
lung and the pericardium. A two-color ﬂow cytometric
study was used to evaluate the expression of CD4 and
CD8 in the tumor-associated lymphocytes, according to a
previously reported method [7], which revealed that 61%
of all lymphoid cells were CD4 /H11001CD8/H11001, the typical phe-
notype of cortical thymocytes ( Fig 2). The postoperative
course was uneventful, and the patient was able to
recover muscle strength to enable her to maintain a
standing or sitting position. She left the hospital 1 month
after the operation; however, painful muscle stiffness
returned 1 month later. Further, a head retraction reﬂex-
like movement evoked by sensory stimulation of the face
appeared, followed by severe bulbar symptoms with
ptosis and dysphagia, which worsened and resulted in
respiratory arrest. A tracheotomy was performed, and
mechanical ventilation was required for 3 months. Al-
though her bulbar symptoms were quite similar to those
of myasthenia gravis (MG), results of serum antiacetyl-
choline receptor (AchR) antibody level and edrophonium
tests were negative. In addition, electromyography
(EMG) did not show a waning phenomenon, which
suggested MG, whereas somatosensory evoked EMG
suggested that her head retraction reﬂex-like movement
was reﬂection of a brainstem disorder associated with
stiff man syndrome, which might have also caused the
bulbar symptoms. These symptoms were relieved after
intravenous immunoglobulin treatment. Two years after
the thymectomy, the symptoms and EMG ﬁndings were
improved without medication, and the level of anti-GAD
antibody had decreased to 9,800 U/mL.
Comment
Three cases of stiff man syndrome associated with a
thymoma have been previously reported [3–5] and, along
with the case reported here, are summarized in Table 1.
These patients in these four cases were two men and two
women, with a mean age of 52 years (range, 40 to 57
years). The anti-GAD antibody, which is associated with
autoimmune diseases, is positive in 60% of patients with
stiff man syndrome, and the antiamphiphysin antibody is
often found in paraneoplastic stiff man syndrome, which
is associated with small cell lung cancer, breast cancer,
colon cancer, and Hodgkin disease [2].I n2o ft h e4
patients with a thymoma, the anti-GAD antibody was
positive, whereas the antiamphiphysin antibody was
negative. A thymectomy was performed in three of those
cases, and the histologic subtypes of the three resected
thymomas were one cortical and two predominantly
lymphocytic types. These histologically deﬁned thymo-
mas are suggested to be type B1 or B2 tumors according
to the WHO histologic classiﬁcation criteria. Further, MG
occurred in 2 of the 4 patients, and 1 patient was positive
for the anti-AchR antibody. The case reported by Nicolas
and colleagues [4] was diagnosed as serologically nega-
tive MG with positive EMG ﬁndings. Bulbar symptoms

are rare in patients with stiff man syndrome; however,
head retraction reﬂex-like movement is suggested to
reﬂect a brainstem disorder, which might cause bulbar
symptoms such as those of MG [8].
In the WHO classiﬁcation, MG is more commonly
associated with type B1 and B2 tumors than other types
[9]. As noted previously, the three thymomas in the
patients with stiff man syndrome were histologically
deﬁned as type B1 or B2. Type B1 and B2 tumors have
abundant CD4 /H11001CD8/H11001T cells, which are supposed to
have some association with the onset of MG. In our case,
two-color ﬂow cytometric analysis revealed an abun-
dance of CD4/H11001CD8/H11001T cells in the tumor. These ﬁndings
seem to suggest that an autoimmune mechanism of stiff
man syndrome with a thymoma may be similar to that of
MG with a thymoma.
In the paraneoplastic stiff man syndrome associated
with breast cancer, small cell lung cancer, Hodgkin
disease, and colon cancer, neurologic symptoms have
been shown to be relieved after tumor treatment [2].I n
the three resected cases mentioned previously, the symp-
toms of stiff man syndrome with a thymoma were alle-
viated after a thymectomy. Therefore, a thymectomy is
considered to be effective treatment of stiff man syn-
drome with a thymoma.
